questions.question: Whitney Houston's 1987 club crossover — which remains one of the most danced-to songs of the decade — was titled what?
choices: Saving All My Love for You
I Wanna Dance with Somebody (Who Loves Me)

metadata.song: I Wanna Dance with Somebody (Who Loves Me)
metadata.fact: 'I Wanna Dance with Somebody (Who Loves Me)' debuted at #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1987 and became one of the decade's defining dance-pop records — its combination of Whitney Houston's vocal power with a propulsive club production made it equally at home in arenas and on dance floors. The song was written by George Merrill and Shannon Rubicam, the same duo behind 'How Will I Know.'
metadata.storyHook: A voice designed for ballads. A production designed for clubs. The combination produced one of 1987's most danced-to records and one of the decade's most enduring reminders that Whitney Houston could do both.
metadata.sourceNotes: Whitney liner notes (Arista Records, 1987). Billboard Hot 100 chart archives. ASCAP songwriting credits.

questions.question: Janet Jackson's 1989 opening salvo from 'Rhythm Nation 1814' — the album's lead dance single — was titled what?

metadata.fact: 'Miss You Much' was the lead single from 'Rhythm Nation 1814' and spent four weeks at #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1989 — it established the album's dance-floor identity before the heavier sociopolitical content of the title track arrived. The choreography that defined the Rhythm Nation era's visual identity was created by Anthony Thomas, while music video director Dominic Sena was responsible for the cinematic framing. Both credits contributed to the song's cultural impact.
metadata.storyHook: The album contained a manifesto about society. Its lead single was a dance record. Janet Jackson understood that you have to get people moving before you can make them think.
metadata.sourceNotes: Rhythm Nation 1814 liner notes (A&M Records, 1989). Billboard Hot 100 chart archives. Anthony Thomas choreography credits. Dominic Sena video direction credits.

questions.question: Ciara's 2005 dance smash — which became her first major Hot 100 breakthrough as a headliner — was titled what?

metadata.fact: '1, 2 Step' reached #4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and featured Missy Elliott — it was Ciara's second single after 'Goodies' and further established her choreography-forward identity. The song's step-counting hook and Ciara's fluid body movement made it one of the decade's most kinetically infectious radio records.
metadata.storyHook: Step one. Step two. The instruction was in the title. Ciara made R&B's most literal dance command into one of 2005's most-played singles.
metadata.sourceNotes: Goodies album liner notes (LaFace Records, 2004). Billboard Hot 100 chart archives. Missy Elliott feature credits.

questions.question: MC Hammer's 1990 Rick James-sampling dance phenomenon — which made parachute pants a cultural artifact — was titled what?

metadata.fact: 'U Can't Touch This' reached #8 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1990 and won the Grammy for Best Rap Solo Performance — it was built on a sample from Rick James's 'Super Freak' and became one of the most recognizable hooks of the decade. MC Hammer's choreography, parachute pants, and self-referential confidence made the song a visual as much as an audio phenomenon.
metadata.storyHook: A sample from Rick James. A hook nobody could get out of their head. Parachute pants that somehow seemed appropriate. MC Hammer's dance identity and the song's production were so perfectly matched that the two became inseparable.
metadata.sourceNotes: Please Hammer, Don't Hurt 'Em liner notes (Capitol Records, 1990). Billboard Hot 100 chart archives. Rick James 'Super Freak' ASCAP sample documentation.

questions.question: Tag Team's 1993 party anthem — which sparked a 'there it is' rivalry with a competing song of nearly identical name — was titled what?

metadata.fact: 'Whoomp! (There It Is)' spent 27 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1993 and competed directly with '95 South's 'Whoot, There It Is' — two Atlanta-area acts releasing near-identically named party records in the same week. Tag Team's version ultimately reached a higher commercial peak, selling over two million copies.

questions.question: Destiny's Child's 2001 dance-floor smash — which coined a new word for a curvaceous body that later entered the dictionary — was titled what?

metadata.fact: 'Bootylicious' sampled Stevie Nicks's 'Edge of Seventeen' guitar riff and reached #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 — the word itself was later accepted into the Oxford English Dictionary. The song's production was a deliberate departure from Destiny's Child's previous sound, with Beyoncé pushing for a harder, guitar-driven dance track.
metadata.storyHook: Destiny's Child sampled Stevie Nicks. The result was a word that made it into the dictionary. The Oxford English Dictionary. 'Bootylicious' is now officially a word and Stevie Nicks's guitar is the reason.
metadata.sourceNotes: Survivor liner notes (Columbia Records, 2001). Billboard Hot 100 chart archives. Oxford English Dictionary word inclusion documentation. Stevie Nicks 'Edge of Seventeen' sample clearance.

questions.question: 'U Can't Touch This' by MC Hammer built its entire groove on a sample from which Rick James track?

bonus.bonusHint: DIGIT 1 OF 3 — THE RICK JAMES TRACK SAMPLED ON U CAN'T TOUCH THIS

metadata.fact: 'Super Freak' was a 1981 Rick James hit on Gordy/Motown Records — MC Hammer's sample was so prominent that James received a co-writing credit on 'U Can't Touch This,' along with royalties that James later described as life-changing. The bassline and hook are essentially unchanged between the two recordings.
metadata.storyHook: Rick James wrote it in 1981. MC Hammer sampled it in 1990. Rick James got a co-writing credit on the song that won the Grammy. He said the royalties changed his life. That is one sample clearance story with a genuinely happy ending.
metadata.sourceNotes: 'U Can't Touch This' ASCAP sample credits (Capitol Records, 1990). Rick James 'Super Freak' discography (Gordy/Motown, 1981). Grammy Award records (33rd ceremony, 1991).

questions.question: Bobby Brown — whose new jack swing style dominated the dance floor in the late 1980s — was born in which Massachusetts city?

metadata.fact: Bobby Brown was born February 5, 1969, in Boston, Massachusetts — he grew up in the Orchard Park projects in Roxbury and was a founding member of New Edition, the Boston boy group whose choreography and new jack swing sensibility shaped his later solo dance identity.
metadata.storyHook: From the Orchard Park projects in Roxbury, Boston. New Edition. Solo career. Bobby Brown's dance-floor dominance traced directly back to a Massachusetts childhood and a group that could move before they could drive.
metadata.sourceNotes: Bobby Brown official biography. New Edition documentation. Roxbury, Boston civic records.

questions.question: MC Hammer's 'U Can't Touch This' — which sampled Rick James's 'Super Freak' — won two Grammys at which ceremony?

metadata.fact: 'U Can't Touch This' won Best Rap Solo Performance and Best R&B Song at the 33rd Grammy Awards in 1991 — making MC Hammer the first rap artist to win multiple Grammys at a single ceremony.
metadata.storyHook: The Grammy was for rap. The audience was pop. MC Hammer won at the intersection of both and made the result look inevitable.

questions.question: 'Bootylicious' — Destiny's Child's genre-defying dance hit — built its groove on the guitar riff of 'Edge of Seventeen' by which rock artist?

metadata.fact: Stevie Nicks's 'Edge of Seventeen' — released in 1982 on Nicks's 'Bella Donna' album — provided the guitar sample that became the rhythmic backbone of 'Bootylicious.' Beyoncé has said that she pushed for the harder, guitar-driven sound specifically because she wanted the song to sound unlike anything Destiny's Child had previously released. Nicks was reportedly delighted by the sampling.
metadata.storyHook: A 1982 Stevie Nicks rock song became the backbone of a 2001 Destiny's Child dance record. The sample crossed genre, decade, and demographic — and produced a word that ended up in the Oxford English Dictionary.
metadata.sourceNotes: Survivor ASCAP sample credits (Columbia Records, 2001). Stevie Nicks 'Edge of Seventeen' discography (Modern Records, 1982). Beyoncé interview documentation.

questions.question: Janet Jackson's 1997 dance-floor tribute 'Together Again' — a jubilant record about reunion — was written as a memorial to friends lost to which epidemic?

metadata.fact: 'Together Again' was written by Janet Jackson, James Harris III, and Terry Lewis as a tribute to friends who had died from AIDS — its production was deliberately euphoric and celebratory rather than mournful, reflecting Jackson's belief that the song should be a joyful reunion fantasy rather than a grief record. The song spent two weeks at #1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
metadata.storyHook: A song about losing people to AIDS that sounds like the best party in the world. Janet Jackson made grief euphoric. The dance floor was the memorial.
metadata.sourceNotes: The Velvet Rope liner notes (Virgin Records, 1997). Billboard Hot 100 chart archives. Janet Jackson interview documentation on AIDS tribute context.

questions.question: MC Hammer's 1991 follow-up album — which contained '2 Legit 2 Quit' and attempted to sustain his commercial momentum — was titled what?

metadata.fact: 'Too Legit to Quit' was released on Capitol Records in October 1991 — it debuted at #1 on the Billboard 200, demonstrating that MC Hammer's commercial machine was still operational after the massive success of 'Please Hammer, Don't Hurt 'Em.' metadata.storyHook: The follow-up to the best-selling rap album of 1990. It debuted at number one. The hand gesture from the music video entered the cultural vocabulary. MC Hammer did not slow down.

metadata.fact: Ciara Princess Harris was born October 25, 1985, in Austin, Texas — she grew up in a military family that moved frequently, eventually settling in the Atlanta area where she was discovered and signed to LaFace Records. questions.question: Before his music career, MC Hammer was a batboy for which Oakland-based Major League Baseball team — befriending players who helped finance his early label?

metadata.fact: MC Hammer worked as a batboy for the Oakland Athletics in the late 1970s, where he befriended players including Reggie Jackson and Mike Davis who later helped fund his independent label Bustin' Records. The Athletics connection gave Hammer early industry exposure and the seed money to record and distribute his debut independently before Capitol Records signed him.
metadata.storyHook: A batboy at the Oakland Coliseum. Reggie Jackson as a mentor. Players funding his first label. MC Hammer's path to 'U Can't Touch This' started in a baseball dugout in Oakland.
metadata.sourceNotes: MC Hammer biographical records. Oakland Athletics historical documentation. Bustin' Records founding documentation.

metadata.fact: George Merrill and Shannon Rubicam wrote both 'How Will I Know' (1985) and 'I Wanna Dance with Somebody (Who Loves Me)' (1987) for Whitney Houston — their second collaboration for her was even more commercially successful than the first. Rubicam and Merrill were a real-life couple who wrote several of the decade's most recognizable pop-R&B crossover records.

questions.question: Tag Team's 'Whoomp! (There It Is)' was released on which Los Angeles-based independent label — founded by Stax Records legend Al Bell — despite the group being Atlanta-bred DJs?

bonus.bonusHint: DIGIT 3 OF 3 — TAG TEAM'S RECORD LABEL

metadata.fact: Bellmark Records was founded by Al Bell — the legendary Stax Records president — and was based in Los Angeles, not Atlanta. Tag Team were Atlanta DJs who worked the city's club circuit, including Magic City, but their record reached national audiences through Bellmark's LA-based independent distribution. The geographic split — Atlanta group, LA label — is one of the period's more notable independent-major crossover stories.
metadata.storyHook: Atlanta DJs. Los Angeles label. Founded by the man who ran Stax Records. Bellmark Records had a more distinguished pedigree than most people knew, and Tag Team got their national platform through it despite being rooted in a completely different city.
metadata.sourceNotes: Tag Team 'Whoomp! (There It Is)' liner notes (Bellmark Records, 1993). Al Bell biographical records. Bellmark Records label history. Stax Records documentation.

reserve.question: MC Hammer's debut independent album — before Capitol Records signed him — was released on which label that he founded himself?

metadata.fact: Bustin' Records was the independent label MC Hammer founded and self-distributed in Oakland — his debut album 'Feel My Power' (1987) was recorded and pressed independently, with distribution funded partly by Oakland Athletics players. Capitol Records A&R discovered the record through its local success and signed Hammer, re-releasing the album as 'Let's Get It Started' before the massive 'Please Hammer, Don't Hurt 'Em' followed.
